questions.q: What is the 'harvest now, decrypt later' threat model?
options: A method RSA uses internally to refresh its own keys periodically
A technique for quantum computers to decrypt data instantly without storing it first
A classical brute-force attack that tries every possible key immediately upon interception
An adversary records encrypted traffic today without decrypting it, then decrypts it retroactively later if a sufficiently capable quantum computer becomes available
questions.explain: Data intercepted and archived now remains a future risk even if no capable quantum computer exists yet, because it can be decrypted retroactively once one does.

questions.q: Why does the lead-time required for cryptographic migration matter, separate from the harvest-now-decrypt-later risk?
options: Migration takes no meaningful time once a new standard is announced
NIST requires a mandatory waiting period of exactly one year before any new standard can be used
Migrating standards across the world's infrastructure historically takes years to over a decade, so starting only once a quantum threat is imminent would mean finishing the migration too late
Lead time only matters for hardware manufacturers, not software or protocol designers
questions.explain: Given how slowly global cryptographic infrastructure typically migrates, proactive action now is necessary to be ready well before any future threat materializes.

questions.q: What are the three NIST post-quantum standards named in this lesson, and what does each do?
options: Only one standard, ML-KEM, covering both encryption and signatures
Shor-KEM, Grover-DSA, and QFT-SIG, three newly invented quantum-native algorithms
RSA-2048, RSA-4096, and AES-256, all upgraded versions of existing classical standards
ML-KEM (key encapsulation, from CRYSTALS-Kyber), ML-DSA (signatures, from CRYSTALS-Dilithium), and SLH-DSA (hash-based signatures, from SPHINCS+)
questions.explain: NIST concluded its initial post-quantum standardization round in 2024 with these three named algorithms, covering key encapsulation and two signature approaches.

questions.q: What is the Learning With Errors (LWE) problem, and why is it relevant to post-quantum cryptography?
options: The problem of recovering a hidden vector from linear equations with added random noise -- believed hard for both classical and quantum computers, forming the basis of lattice-based schemes like ML-KEM and ML-DSA
A measurement error that occurs during Shor's algorithm's phase estimation step
The classical error rate of RSA key generation hardware
A synonym for the General Number Field Sieve's running time
questions.explain: LWE's hardness (recovering a hidden vector despite deliberately added noise) is the security foundation for lattice-based post-quantum algorithms.

questions.q: Why doesn't Shor's algorithm threaten lattice-based problems like LWE the way it threatens RSA's factoring problem?
options: LWE problems are always solved using Shor's algorithm itself, just with different inputs
Lattice-based cryptography avoids modular arithmetic entirely, which is why it is immune to all known attacks
Shor's algorithm has already been proven to break LWE just as efficiently as it breaks RSA
Shor's algorithm's speedup exploits periodic structure present in factoring and discrete-log problems; LWE does not have that same periodic structure for the algorithm to exploit
questions.explain: Shor's period-finding reduction relies on periodic structure that factoring and discrete-log have; LWE's hardness rests on a different structural problem that quantum algorithms have not been shown to exploit similarly.
